title: Structural impediments to safety goals and risk-informed regulation in Japan
abstract: In Japan, safety goals and risk-informed regulation (RIR) have been discussed for decades as approaches to improving the transparency, coherence, and consistency of nuclear regulation. Although probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) was introduced in the 1990s and draft safety goals were proposed in the early 2000s, safety goals have not been institutionalized, and the practical application of RIR remains limited. This study examines the structural impediments that have hindered the institutionalization of safety goals and the increased use of RIR in Japan. Based on a literature review, the historical development of safety goals, PRA, and risk-informed applications in Japanese nuclear regulation is summarized. The impediments are then analyzed from four perspectives: legal and institutional, technical, economic, and cultural. Legally, the regulatory framework does not clearly specify how safety goals should be related to the licensing criterion of ensuring “not hinder the prevention of disasters” under the Reactor Regulation Act, limiting their use in regulatory decisions. Technically, the long-standing limitation of PRA applications, particularly regarding external events, together with challenges in the treatment of uncertainty, has reduced the acceptability of PRA as a basis for regulatory judgments. Economically, weak incentives for sustained investment in PRA have constrained progress. As a cultural impediment, a tendency to preserve the Safety Myth has fostered a cautious attitude toward the quantification and disclosure of accident risks, further constraining progress. This study concludes that the interaction of these factors has formed a vicious circle, impeding the institutionalization of safety goals and the increased use of RIR in Japan.

title: Reactor physics and thermal hydraulics analysis of lead-cooled fast reactors
abstract: Lead-cooled Fast Reactors (LFR) have been identified as one of the six promising reactor types for the future of nuclear energy by the Generation IV International Forum. Worldwide, there is an important interest in the use of heavy liquid metals, lead or alloys of lead, as coolants due to their favorable thermal and neutronic characteristics. The development of LFR opens exciting opportunities for innovation in design and brings new challenges in licensing for deployment and commercial operation. This special issue presents papers in the area of Lead Fast Reactor technology, focusing on engineering and design aspects within the scope of the journal. A total of 20 research articles were published about: (a) Numerical modelling and extensive use of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) for the analysis and design of LFR; (b) Adaptation and coupling of best estimate codes for the analysis and design of LFR; (c) Experimental facilities that enable, first and foremost, the acquisition of experimental data and the generation of benchmark-type applications, which are fundamental in the validation of numerical codes; (d) Expansion strategies in nuclear energy generation with light water reactors and small modular reactors (case Netherlands); (e) Development of upscaled numerical models to simulate the behavior of neutron and thermohydraulic processes at the reactor scale (case Mexico); (f) Safety of compact lead-cooled pool fast reactors in seismic events; g) Multiphase phenomena for evaluating Steam Generator Tube Rupture (SGTR) risks in Lead-cooled Fast Reactors; h) Analysis of pool thermal-hydraulic phenomena in heavy-liquid metal systems, combining experimental research with numerical simulations.

title: Reliability-Based Optimization of Concrete Gamma-Ray Shielding Thickness: A Methodological Framework for 137Cs Sources
abstract: Reliable gamma-ray shielding design requires balancing radiological protection and construction costs while accounting for uncertainties in source characteristics, material properties, and geometry. This study presents a reliability-based optimization framework for determining the optimum thickness of homogeneous concrete shielding against gamma radiation from a hypothetical 137 Cs point source. The dose-response model combines exponential attenuation with the ANSI/ANS-6.4.3 geometric-progression (GP) buildup formulation. Uncertainties in source activity, gamma-dose constant, concrete density, shielding thickness, and source-to-receptor distances are incorporated into a probabilistic limit-state function. Dose-limit exceedance probabilities are evaluated using the First-Order Reliability Method (FORM), Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS), and Weighted Average Simulation Method (WASM). Life-cycle cost optimization is performed using the Golden Section Search (GSS) and compared with the Firefly Algorithm (FA). A comprehensive parametric investigation examines the effects of benchmark reliability levels, receptor distance, annual release probability, service life, discount rate, and economic consequence ratio. Experimental comparisons with published 137 Cs transmission measurements indicate conservative GP predictions under normal incidence, while revealing limitations associated with oblique irradiation. The numerical methods show close agreement, with FORM providing substantial computational advantages. Optimum shielding thickness is governed primarily by reliability requirements and receptor distance, whereas economic parameters become more influential at lower reliability levels. A database comprising 116,640 optimum solutions supports reliability-based design charts and sensitivity analyses. The proposed framework provides a practical basis for preliminary shielding optimization, although its quantitative predictions remain dependent on the adopted source geometry and attenuation assumptions.

title: Long-term high-sensitivity operation of a reprogrammable floating-gate MOS dosimeter: Gamma irradiation and a non-ionizing UV control
abstract: Commercial electrically programmable analog devices (EPADs) based on a reprogrammable floating-gate MOS structure were operated in a high-sensitivity ( HighSens ) regime, in which two devices on the same ALD1108E chip alternate between radiation monitoring and electrical recharging of the floating gate. Long-term experiments were performed under 6 0 ⁢ C o gamma irradiation and under 311 nm UV exposure using matched cycling and reprogramming protocols. Under zero-bias gamma irradiation, HighSens operation provided a near-linear reconstructed dose response with a sensitivity of 8 . 9 5 m V / G y up to 560 Gy, without functional failure. Static positive bias and negative bias produced a progressive loss of reprogramming efficiency and eventual failure to restore the target threshold voltage. A matched zero-bias UV control, in which 311 nm photons discharge the floating gate without generating electron–hole pairs in S i O 2 , showed stable reprogramming jumps and no device failure over a larger equivalent-dose range. The comparison indicates that the long-term degradation of reprogramming efficiency under gamma irradiation is associated with ionizing-radiation effects in combination with repeated electrical stress, rather than with electrical stress alone.

title: Enhancing the nuclear safety regulatory framework and technical standards for maritime non-light-water SMRs
abstract: The 2023 net-zero-by-2050 greenhouse-gas strategy of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has renewed interest in nuclear propulsion at sea, and Korea is advancing non-light-water small modular reactors (SMRs) for ship propulsion and floating power generation. Korea’s Nuclear Safety Act, however, licenses only light- and heavy-water reactors on fixed land sites. This study surveys marine nuclear regulation in ten nations, keeping only issues common to five or more and beyond unilateral competence, and tests the Nuclear Safety Act against the Ship Safety Act. Seven such issues are identified: the 1981 IMO Code’s pressurized-water-reactor premise; the lack of legal status for non-self-propelled floating plants; the undefined nuclear–maritime division of jurisdiction; exclusion of ship-installed reactors from civil-liability regimes; port entry approval; dual licensing; and the demonstration–regulation vicious cycle. Revision of the IMO Code, targeted for 2030, is the global critical path. Fourteen further issues are traced through the marine-specific life-cycle stages—siting and installation, operation, maintenance, decommissioning—each remedy assigned to a named instrument. A three-part test for the limits of delegated legislation shows that seven of the remedies proposed—six of the fourteen, together with the allocation of ministerial jurisdiction—require prior amendment of the parent statute, fixing the order of reform.

title: Comparison of 1-D and 3-D simulations and parametric study of a steady state natural circulation loop with internal heat generating fluid
abstract: In liquid-fueled molten salt reactors (MSRs), decay heat is generated volumetrically within the fuel salt and is distributed throughout the circulation loop following reactor shutdown. This internal heat generation (IHG) can alter the buoyancy distribution and heat removal characteristics of the natural circulation loop (NCL), resulting in significantly different behavior compared to that observed in a conventional NCL with a localized heater. In this study, a geometry-dependent 1-D steady-state model was developed for an NCL with IHG. To assess the applicability and limitations of the proposed 1-D model, 3-D CFD simulations were performed over laminar to turbulent flow regimes. The 1-D model predicted the steady-state Reynolds number ( Re ss ) within a 7% difference from the CFD results in the turbulent regime, whereas relatively larger discrepancies were observed in the laminar and transitional regimes. Detailed CFD analysis showed that IHG induced local buoyancy effects and increased the overall flow resistance, causing the 1-D model to overpredict the Re ss in the laminar regime. This overprediction may lead to an underestimation of the maximum fluid temperature, resulting in non-conservative thermal predictions for MSR passive heat removal systems. Based on this assessment, reactor-scale IHG-NCL analyses were conducted using the 1-D model only in the turbulent regime, by varying the cooler length and cooler position. These findings clarify the range of applicability of the 1-D model assumptions in IHG-NCL modeling and provide guidance for cooler geometry design in MSR applications.

title: Robust identification of unseen radionuclide mixtures using compact structured representations
abstract: Identifying previously unseen combinations of known radionuclides in low-resolution gamma-ray spectrometry remains challenging under spectral degradation and varying acquisition conditions. This study evaluates three multi-label architectures—1D-CNN, AE+MLP, and Hilbert-AE+MLP—for radionuclide-mixture identification under controlled spectral perturbations and domain shifts. A dataset of 4,158 MCNP6-simulated spectra, covering six radionuclides and all 63 non-empty compositions, was generated using a 2″ × 2″ NaI(Tl) detector model. Composition-level partitioning and six-fold cross-validation were used to assess generalization to previously unseen compositions. Under ideal conditions, the F1-scores were 0.984 ± 0.033, 0.998 ± 0.005, and 0.997 ± 0.006 for 1D-CNN, AE+MLP, and Hilbert-AE+MLP, respectively. Under spectral perturbations, Hilbert-AE+MLP showed consistent performance across the tested gain-displacement and resolution-degradation conditions, achieving an F1-score of 0.889 ± 0.003 under 12.0% resolution degradation and ±15% gain displacement without retraining. On strictly unseen experimental compositions, it achieved precision, recall, and F1-score of 1.00, while its mean per-isotope F1-score on strictly unseen short-time compositions was 0.690 ± 0.009. Controlled comparisons and locality analysis indicate that the observed robustness is associated with structured preservation of local spectral neighborhoods in the Hilbert representation.

title: Optimization of the retrieval-augmented generation workflow for question answering on nuclear safety regulations
abstract: The baseline retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflow often fails to meet the specific needs of high-stakes domains such as question answering (Q&A) for nuclear safety regulations. To improve answer accuracy, multiple strategies have been adopted to optimize the retrieval, query and generation stages of the RAG workflow. The Q&A performance under different single-stage, dual-stage, and three-stage RAG optimization strategies have been compared. The Q&A performance under all 2048 possible RAG workflow configurations has been exhaustively evaluated, and the top-ranked workflows have been tested on self-constructed QA datasets. The results indicate that the RAG-based Q&A system significantly outperforms general large language models (LLMs), and the three-stage optimized RAG workflow achieves substantially higher answer accuracy than the baseline.

title: Numerical research on response of fluid-induced vibration of reactor core barrel
abstract: : The flow-induced vibration analysis of the reactor core barrel is very important for the safe operation of the reactor. Based on the theory of power spectral density (PSD) analysis for random vibration and the previous research on hydrodynamic loads on the surface of core barrel, a set of analytical method for calculating the flow-induced vibration response of core barrel of the pressurized water reactor is proposed in this paper. Firstly, the finite element model (FEM) of core barrel was established, including the setting of appropriate constraint conditions and the calculation of the additional mass of the structure in water. Secondly, the correlation length of core barrel was calculated based on the load data. And the load spectrum on the surface of core barrel was constructed according to our previous research. Thirdly, based on the ANSYS Program, the PSD spectrum analysis of random vibration under multiple groups of dense frequencies was completed respectively. Finally, the combination of Square Root of the Sum of the Squares (SRSS) about the spectrum analysis results of each group was carried out. To verify the analytical method, a flow-induced vibration response test of the reactor core barrel was conducted. According to research, the theoretical results are approximately 40% higher than the experimental measurements. The sensitivity analysis of the correlation length indicates that the magnitude of flow-induced vibration response is directly proportional to the magnitude of the correlation length.

title: Joint optimization of analysis-unit selection and scored cell number for AI-assisted dicentric chromosome biodosimetry
abstract: Background Rapid biological dose assessment is essential for radiation emergency response, but AI-assisted dicentric chromosome analysis requires explicit selection of valid analysis units and determination of a scored cell number. Their interdependence remains unclear. Methods Dicentric chromosome assay data obtained under acute whole-body gamma-ray exposure conditions were evaluated using retention criteria based on the mode ± K median absolute deviations of the chromosome-count distribution (K = 2–9). At each criterion, 1,000 bootstrap iterations quantified dose variability. The required scored cell number was defined as the earliest point at which agreement in the coefficient of variation was sustained at ≥ 97 %. Results Dose variability decreased as the scored cell number increased, with diminishing gains from additional scoring. K = 2 retained 64.5 % of analysis units, whereas newly included units decreased from 6.4 % at K = 3 to 1.3 % at K = 9. Broadening the retention criterion minimally changed the required scored cell number or estimated dose but generally widened the 95 % confidence interval. Conclusion Joint optimization of analysis-unit selection and scored cell number provides a basis for balancing scoring efficiency and analytical burden against dose-estimation uncertainty, supporting resource-efficient biological dosimetry during large-scale radiation emergency response.

title: Interpretable machine learning-aided mix design of uranium tailings-based geopolymers: strength, microstructure and radon exhalation
abstract: : Mix design of alkali-activated uranium tailings-based geopolymers still relies on trial and error, hindering low-carbon solidification of radioactive tailings. Here, geopolymer monoliths were fabricated from uranium tailings, ground granulated blast-furnace slag, silica fume and fly ash, and assessed through single-factor and L16(4 5 ) orthogonal experiments, XRD, FTIR, SEM-EDS, closed-chamber radon measurement and explainable machine learning. A dense amorphous C-(A)-S-H/zeolitic gel formed and acted as the primary binder; the maximum 28-day unconfined compressive strength reached 29.01 MPa. Radon exhalation fell by 96.6–99.4% relative to raw tailings, keeping every mix 14–79 times below the EJ/T 977-95 screening limit. XGBoost outperformed four benchmark models under repeated cross-validation (holdout R 2 = 0.923), and SHAP analysis recovered a factor hierarchy consistent with orthogonal range analysis and microstructural evidence. Surrogate optimization and design of experiments converged on one recipe (activator modulus 1.4, liquid–solid ratio 0.20, alkali equivalent 12%, modified material dosage 15%); a confirmatory cast validated this recommendation, its 28-day strength falling within the bootstrap prediction interval and its radon exhalation the lowest of all mixes. This workflow provides a low-carbon, interpretable route to intelligent mix design for radioactive-waste solidification.

title: Application of cosine similarity analysis for monitoring the recovery of mobile inspection radiation sources
abstract: In mobile radiation monitoring equipment, there is a risk of loss of radiation source during transport and field work. In order to mitigate the risk of loss of radiation source in mobile radiographic operation, this study proposes a dynamic monitoring approach based on Cosine Similarity Analysis for real-time tracking the location of radioactive sources during recovery process. In this method, real-time radiation dose rate data is continuously collected throughout the source deployment and recovery phases using a mobile radiographic system. Measured point - Dose rate distribution curves are then constructed and cosine similarity algorithms are employed to quantify the spatial distribution consistency between the deployment and recovery dose rate profiles. Experimental validation was conducted under normal recovery conditions as well as three Source-Drop scenarios occurring at the container exit, along the transfer path and at the inspection site. By employing a Sliding-Window algorithm to dynamically compute cosine similarity, the proposed method enables real-time detection of significant decreases in similarity, thereby achieving precise identification of source drop location. In addition, robustness analysis was performed to establish a three-level risk criterion for classifying operational risk. Through a combined analysis of data obtained during the deployment and recovery phases, the proposed method provides a highly responsive and accurate intelligent early-warning mechanism for monitoring the status of mobile radiographic sources. The method effectively reduces the probability of source loss in field operations and enhances the efficiency of source retrieval, demonstrating substantial potential for engineering applications in radiation safety management.

title: Euler–Euler simulation of flow-induced vibrations of an obstacle in two-phase pipe flow
abstract: Understanding Flow-Induced Vibrations (FIV) is essential for ensuring the safety of steam generators in nuclear power plants. Unchecked vibrations can cause tube wear, fatigue or even failure, posing potential safety risks. In U-tube configurations where two-phase cross-flow is prevalent, these issues become more severe. While this phenomenon has been thoroughly examined in single-phase cross-flow, its behavior in two-phase flows is less understood. The Horizon Europe project GO-VIKING aims to tackle these issues by utilizing experimental setups to investigate two-phase flow-induced vibrations. These facilities emphasize the Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) between tube bundles and air–water cross-flows. This paper presents both classical and hybrid Euler–Euler simulations of FIV of a cylindrical obstacle in two-phase pipe flow, as recently experimentally studied in the PILULE experiment performed by Electricité de France R&D. The emphasis of this work lies on the assessment of the two-phase modeling methodology itself, with the flow-induced vibration of the obstacle serving as an application and validation case. The LogMoM model is used for the poly-disperse bubble distribution, including advanced closure models for coalescence and break-up. Particularly in the wake of the obstacle, coalescence and break-up play an important role in the redistribution of void. In turn, drag and lift forces acting on the obstacle are predicted. The presented work contributes to establishing a validated two-phase flow FSI simulation strategy of FIV in cross-flows over tube bundles. The paper demonstrates the shortcomings of both the classical model, which fails to capture large bubbles and pressure fluctuations, and the hybrid model, which is seen to produce fluctuations but is too aggressive in its transition to resolved bubbles. This shows that further developments are needed in terms of pressure fluctuation modeling as well as fundamental hybrid model improvements.

title: Development of surrogate model for reactor cooling system based on ASTEC simulations during the early phase of station blackout
abstract: In this work, metamodels capable of reproducing the thermal-hydraulic behavior of subsystems of the reactor coolant system (RCS) during the early phase of a Station Blackout (SBO) leading to a severe accident—i.e., up to the point of fission product release in the RCS—are proposed as a first step toward the development of accelerated surrogate models for severe accident simulations. The work is performed in the frame of the EU-funded project ASSAS, which aims at developing a basic-principles severe accident simulator for a generic 1300 MW pressurized water reactor (PWR), by replacing ASTEC (severe accident code developed by ASNR) models with Machine Learning (ML) surrogate models. The work presented here focuses on the thermal-hydraulic CESAR module for the primary and secondary circuits. A suitable training dataset must be generated. A base case scenario is considered, involving an SBO without any safety measures until the onset of fission product release. From this base case, various calculations are performed by depressurizing remotely the primary circuit at different times, followed by the recovery of emergency water injection, also at different times. From these ASTEC calculations only the variables needed for the surrogate model development are extracted. These include state variables for each control volume within the RCS domain, boundary conditions, and additional variables that may provide information about the overall evolution of the accident and could be useful for ML. The surrogate models are expected to compute each time step while also accounting for user decisions interactively during the accident simulation. The ML method considered here is based on Recurrent Neural Networks, which are commonly used for time series. The developed LSTM-based surrogate models achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) on the order of 10 −3 on an independent test dataset. Temperatures and steam pressures were predicted with the highest accuracy, whereas void fractions and hydrogen partial pressures exhibited larger errors. Among the four metamodels, the steam generator secondary side showed the most robust predictive performance, while the primary side was more sensitive to rare events. Larger error metrics were especially found during changes in operational state.

title: Age-Dependent Health Risk Assessment of Uranium in Drinking Water from Mining-Affected Regions of Bikaner and the Aravalli Hills of Jhunjhunu District, Rajasthan, India
abstract: Fresh ground water is essential for human consumption and agricultural irrigation however in arid and mining areas the fresh groundwater may be contaminated with uranium. High uranium concentration in drinking water is a big concern due to both the radiological and chemical toxicity potential health risks. The mobility and transport of uranium in groundwater may be affected by mining and local hydrogeologic conditions, hence need for site-specific investigations and in-depth health risk assessments. The present study investigates uranium concentration in groundwater samples collected from various mining-affected areas of Bikaner and Aravalli Hills and Khetri regions of Jhunjhunu districts in northern Rajasthan India. One hundred groundwater samples were collected from 20 different locations at different depths, with five individual samples taken from each location. Uranium concentration was analyzed by LED fluorimeter along with water chemistry—pH, electrical conductance (EC), total dissolved solids (TDS). Health risks were estimated separately using age-dependent annual effective dose (AED) calculations for radiological exposure and lifetime average daily dose (LADD) and hazard quotient (HQ) for chemical toxicity. The results indicate that uranium concentrations vary between 28.1 ± 3 to 172.7 ± 15 µg/L. Nineteen out of twenty location-wise mean concentrations exceed the WHO and USEPA guideline of 30 µg/L and a strong correlation coefficient was observed with groundwater depth (r = 0.866, R2 = 0.7494, p < .001), TDS (r = 0.91, R2 = 0.8302, p < .001) and electrical conductivity (r = 0.86, R2 = 0.7492, p < .001). Infants receive the highest AED doses among all age groups however all doses are below than ICRP reference value of 1 mSv/y. HQ values exceed the WHO, 2026 guidelines of one at all locations while LADD values vary between 0.80 and 4.93 µg/kg·day, indicating potential chemical toxicity risks. Hence groundwater collected from mining-impacted areas has higher concentrations of uranium than drinking-water guideline values indicate greater chemical toxicity health risks than radiological impacts. These findings indicate that 19 out of the 20 location-wise mean concentrations exceed the WHO and USEPA recommend value of 30 µg/L, and eight out of 20 exceeds the AERB prescribed value the 60 µg/L. The estimated radiological doses for all the age groups are below the recommended dose value as given by ICRP, however indicating a higher chemical (nephrotoxic) toxicity risk due to HQ values exceed the WHO, 2026 guidelines of one at all locations. The statistical correlation between the concentration of uranium and groundwater depth, TDS, and electrical conductivity indicates that uranium concentrations may increase with increase these physiochemical parameters. Further hydrochemical characterization, additional seasonal sampling, and uncertainty in exposure assumptions are needed for further work to refine the uranium assessment. Remediation and regular monitoring of drinking-water sources are recommended to reduce the exposure risk in affected locations.

title: Neutron Irradiation in Thermoelectrics for Space Nuclear Power: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: Thermoelectric generators are critical solid-state energy converters in space nuclear power systems, where their long-term operational stability under neutron irradiation critically determines mission lifetime.This review presents a systematic overview of neutron irradiation effects on established thermoelectric materials (e.g., Bi 2 Te 3 , PbTe, SiGe) and emerging candidates (e.g., half-Heuslers, skutterudites, Zintl phases). We systematically analyze experimental data on the evolution of electrical conductivity, Seebeck coefficient, and thermal conductivity, revealing the complex interplay among neutron fluence, energy spectrum, and irradiation temperature. Building upon empirical trends, we develop a multi-scale framework linking microscopic damage events to macroscopic degradation of thermoelectric transport properties. We further evaluate the efficacy of post-irradiation recovery strategies, including annealing and in situ thermal recovery. Finally, we identify critical pathways for future research, emphasizing the rational design of irradiation-tolerant materials via microstructural engineering and composition optimization, the development of predictive models coupling defect dynamics to performance, and the advancement of in situ characterization techniques for extreme environments. This review aims to establish a foundational knowledge base and a strategic roadmap for advancing high-reliability thermoelectrics toward next-generation space explorations and terrestrial nuclear energy applications.

title: Modeling the separation of silicon isotopes in square cascades: Impact of material losses and light gas production
abstract: This study investigates isotopic separation and concentration distributions within a square cascade to assess the effects of material losses and light HF gas generation. A computational model was developed for this analysis, focusing on four key parameters in cascades with 50 and 25 stages: stage feed rate, P/F ratio, cascade feed, and unit separation factor, specifically for the SiF4 isotope mixture. The results reveal that the cascade feed rate, stage feed rate, and P/F ratio significantly influence the HF concentration in the light product at the final stage, particularly under conditions of high material losses. Notably, all HF gas is directed towards the end of the cascade, leading to a sudden increase in concentration in the light product at the final stage. Furthermore, the extent of material losses and the accumulation of HF gas in the last stage increase with the number of stages in the cascade. As the material loss coefficient rises, the isotopic separation of the target isotope in longer cascades diminishes compared to shorter ones. Additionally, increased material losses result in a reduced depletion of the light isotope at the end of the heavy product, contributing to a greater overall loss of the target isotope.

title: Physics-informed neural surrogates for joint spent-fuel decay heat and pool thermal screening
authors: Bruno Rucy Carneiro Alves de Lima
abstract: • Includes a 20,000-case spent-fuel decay heat and pool thermal response benchmark. • Physics-informed networks penalize thermal and decay-heat inconsistencies. • Joint in-distribution normalized error is 52.2 % below the standard neural ensemble. • The selected model reaches 9.25 % mean absolute percentage error on calorimetry. Rapid spent fuel pool (SFP) assessment requires fast, reliable estimates of decay heat and thermal response across heterogeneous fuel inventories and degraded cooling states. This study establishes a new, reproducible benchmark by sampling three-cohort pressurized water reactor spent-fuel inventories, deriving decay heat from an open Serpent2 depletion library, and propagating the resulting heat load through a reduced-order subcooled pool energy balance. The proposed physics-informed neural network (PINN) embeds heat-balance consistency, physically correct transient direction, and decay-heat monotonicity into supervised learning. These constraints directly couple the heat-load and temperature targets and discourage physically inconsistent predictions under domain shift. To the authors’ knowledge, this is the first openly reproducible study to evaluate a problem-specific PINN for joint SFP decay-heat and bulk-temperature prediction using independent calorimetry and explicit domain-shift tests. The latter is compared on independent and identically distributed (IID) and domain-shift conditions with engineering and statistical baselines, multilayer perceptron (MLP) ensembles, physics-feature MLPs and decay-heat residual hybrids. Architectures and hyperparameters are selected using validation scores; performance is assessed through repeated holdouts and external CLAB calorimetry. Direct Serpent interpolation achieves 5.65 % MAPE on 16 measured 17 × 17 CLAB assemblies, reduced to 1.73 % by the reported 27.1 W bias correction. Across five random seeds, the selected PINN MLP attains an IID mean normalized RMSE of 0.031, reducing IID mean normalized RMSE by 52.2 % relative to the standard MLP ensemble, while achieving 9.25 % external decay-heat MAPE. The results demonstrate that problem-specific physics constraints materially improve rapid, simultaneous heat-load and thermal-response prediction.

title: Development of a one-dimensional thermal–hydraulics framework for nuclear reactor analysis in OpenFOAM
abstract: Modern nuclear reactor safety analyses increasingly rely on multi-fidelity approaches, combining high-resolution CFD and porous-medium models in localized regions with lower-fidelity system thermal–hydraulic models for full-plant simulations. Within this hierarchy, one-dimensional system codes are essential, capturing entire reactor circuits at a fraction of the cost of higher-fidelity methods. In this context, the foamForNuclear platform has recently been developed as an OpenFOAM-based multi-physics, multi-fidelity framework enabling the coupling of porous-medium and CFD regions within a unified environment. However, it lacks a native 1D thermal–hydraulic capability and therefore depends on external system codes for plant-scale analyses, limiting full integration within the OpenFOAM ecosystem. This work presents a new OpenFOAM-native 1D thermal–hydraulic framework fully integrated into FFN. To the authors’ knowledge, this is the first such implementation embedded directly within OpenFOAM and designed for consistent coupling with higher-fidelity models. The formulation is based on 1D conservation equations for mass, momentum, and energy, representing pipes, junctions, pumps, and hydraulic discontinuities, and is currently restricted to single-phase flow. Component-level verification against analytical solutions shows very good agreement for hydraulic and thermal test cases. System-level performance is assessed using a representative reactor-circuit transient and compared against the system code TRACE, showing good agreement in pressure, flow redistribution, and temperature evolution. This work establishes a consistent foundation for OpenFOAM-native system thermal–hydraulics within FFN and enables future extensions to advanced multi-physics applications, including two-phase flow modelling.

title: Tangential gas injection-enhanced fuel elements for centrifugal nuclear thermal rockets: A thermal-hydraulic analysis
abstract: This study proposes the application of tangential hydrogen injection as an alternative swirl-generation concept for centrifugal nuclear thermal rocket (CNTR) fuel elements and numerically evaluates its gas-side thermal-hydraulic performance. Two swirl-generation mechanisms are investigated: tangential inlet-induced (TII) swirl, produced by tangential hydrogen injection, and wall rotation-induced (WRI) swirl, produced by mechanically rotating boundaries. A two-dimensional axisymmetric-swirl unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (URANS) framework with Reynolds Stress Model (RSM) turbulence closure was validated against experimental swirling-flow data and subsequently applied to compare the two configurations under matched swirl intensity, inlet mass flow rate, geometry, and thermal boundary conditions. The results show fundamentally different radial swirl distributions: TII produces a Rankine-vortex-type flow with swirl concentrated toward the core and decaying downstream, whereas WRI maintains a forced-vortex-type flow with strong near-wall tangential motion. At the baseline condition of 200 RPM-equivalent swirl and a wall heat flux of 3000 W/m 2 , TII increases the global Nusselt number from 10.63 to 12.66, corresponding to an approximately 19% enhancement over WRI, while producing nearly identical pressure loss. Increasing the imposed swirl from 100 to 600 RPM-equivalent increases the global Nusselt number of TII from 11.50 to 16.48, whereas that of WRI remains nearly unchanged. The resulting Figure of Merit (FoM) for TII increases from approximately 1.06 to 1.63. The radial pressure differences generated by TII and WRI are comparable near the injection region, indicating that both mechanisms generate centrifugal fields that may contribute to fuel retention; however, the TII-induced field decays downstream while the WRI field is continuously sustained by wall rotation. Overall, the results demonstrate the potential of TII for enhancing gas-side heat transfer while generating a centrifugal field and potentially reducing reliance on mechanically rotating components in CNTR fuel elements. Further, two-phase simulations, injector-geometry and outlet-orifice optimization, and system-level analyses are required to determine its feasibility under representative CNTR operating conditions.

title: Co-occurrence of Elevated Natural Radioactivity and Potentially Toxic Elements in Laboni Beach Sands: Source Provenance and Radiological Hazards Assessment
abstract: This study first reported high levels of naturally occurring radionuclides 226Ra (460 Bq/kg) and 232Th (838 Bq/kg) in Laboni Beach, compared to world average and other coastal beaches in Bangladesh. Twenty-five sand samples were collected to determine natural radionuclides (226Ra, 232Th and 40K) using the HPGe gamma spectrometry. To understand the origin of radioactive sources, the elements of heavy metals meticulously studied by FAAS absorption spectrophotometer and ICP-OES optical emission spectroscopy, where Fe, Mn, Cr, Cd, As, Sb, and Se were found to be 1.48, 1.15, 2.25, 29.3, 1.29, 1.9, and 5.54 times higher than the earth’s continental crust values. The co-occurrence of natural radionuclides (226Ra and 232Th) with Pb, Cu, Cd, and Fe suggests their enrichment from a common geogenic source through heavy mineral concentration. Elevated 232Th/226Ra (mean: 1.85, 2.2 × world average), 232Th/40K (mean: 4.02, 57.4 × world average), and 226Ra/40K (mean: 2.21, 2.5 × world average) ratios, corroborated by statistical analyses and source apportionment model, confirm the predominance of Th-rich heavy-mineral assemblages and their control on the enrichment of natural radionuclides and associated heavy metals. The predominance of Cadmium (Cd) and Chromium (Cr) in the ecological risk index identifies as the principal ecological risk factors. Radiological health risk evaluation demonstrated that all hazard indices exceeded the recommended safety limits, underscoring significant public health concerns for local residents, tourists, and the use of beach sands as construction materials.

title: Assessment of the 3D Pressure Drop Tensor Formulation in Porous Media for Tube Bundle Configurations
abstract: Porous media modeling is often retained in the nuclear industry for the thermal-hydraulics component scale simulation of the core and of steam generators. In this approach, the fuel/tube bundle solid boundaries are not explicitly simulated, and their presence is modeled by a volume porosity and a pressure drop source term in the momentum equations, the goal of which is to describe the forces induced by the structures on the flow. This paper attempts to assess the consistency of the pressure drop formulation in 3D cylinder bundle configurations. The first part of the paper describes the possible tensor formulations and proposes a simple test case to show potential weaknesses in reproducing experimental data. For the tensor formulations tested, it was not possible to obtain the pressure drop corresponding to the correlation value, for angles of the flow different than 0 and 90 deg with respect to the tube direction. In the second part of the paper, a 3D external single-phase flow across an oblique tube bundle is considered: the tube bundle is made of 20 × 20 triangular-pitch straight tubes, with a 45-deg angle between the tubes and the free stream. This configuration was simulated through both a porous media and a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) approach (RANS). CFD results are averaged along control volumes representative of the porous media simulation scale. The velocity profiles calculated by the two approaches are compared along different profiles inside the tube bundle: regions with different flow deviation predicted by the two approaches are identified.

title: Oxide Growth and Recrystallization Behavior of CANDU Zircaloy-4 Cladding during Accelerated Air Oxidation
abstract: Accelerated air oxidation tests were conducted on CANDU spent fuel claddings to determine a practical acceleration criterion for simulated dry-storage specimens. The mechanical integrity of the oxidized cladding was also evaluated after accelerated oxidation. The oxidation tests were performed at 400, 420, and 450 °C in air until oxide layers exceeding 10 μm were formed. Oxide growth, mechanical integrity, and recrystallization behavior were assessed through microstructural characterization, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and ring compression tests (RCT). All conditions successfully generated oxide layers exceeding 10 μm. XRD analysis confirmed predominantly monoclinic ZrO 2 with minor tetragonal ZrO 2 near the oxide/metal interface. RCT results revealed that all oxidized specimens maintained ductility without brittle fracture, indicating that oxidation up to 10 μm did not significantly degrade mechanical integrity. However, recrystallization behavior strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. The as-received microstructure was retained at 400 °C, whereas partial and significant recrystallization occurred at 420 °C and 450 °C, respectively. An EBSD-based time–temperature recrystallization boundary map revealed that recrystallization onset during oxidation to a 10 μm oxide layer occurs at approximately 406 °C. Considering practical uncertainties, 400 °C was determined to be the practical acceleration temperature limit for producing representative simulated dry-storage specimens.

title: Experimental investigation for monitoring axial preload degradation in a scaled-down core support barrel
abstract: The core support barrel (CSB) is continuously forced into lateral motion by the hydraulic load of the incoming coolant and flow-induced vibration (FIV) in the annular downcomer. This motion has been diagnosed via ex-core neutron noise analysis, and the loss of axial preload was identified as the physical factor that relates to the lateral vibration. This loss of preload is primarily attributed to degradation of the hold-down ring and a non-uniform axial preload distribution. In operating nuclear power plants, ex-core neutron noise is monitored through the Internals Vibration Monitoring System (IVMS). However, clear quantitative action criteria have not yet been established. From the perspective of condition monitoring and prognostics, a quantitative index is required to diagnose axial preload variations. In this study, the reduction in axial preload was simulated stepwise on a scaled CSB mock-up that reproduces the load path of the flange fastening region that constitutes the boundary condition of the CSB, and the resulting variations in the first beam mode frequency were investigated by experimental modal analysis (EMA). On this basis, a trend analysis was conducted to monitor the axial preload reduction caused by local and global degradation, through which a monitoring guideline applicable to long-term surveillance was proposed.

title: A Modelica-Based Dynamic Model of a Novel Two-Loop Coupled Configuration for the NHR200-II
abstract: A Modelica-based dynamic model is developed for a novel two-loop configuration of the NHR200-II steam supply system. By eliminating the intermediate isolation loop, the proposed configuration increases saturated steam pressure from 1.6 to 3.2 MPa and temperature from 201.4 to 237.4 °C, while retaining primary-loop natural circulation. The model integrates reactor kinetics, thermal hydraulics, and control components within Modelica's modular, equation-based framework. Steady-state comparisons with design data show a maximum relative deviation of 1.03%. Dynamic comparison with RELAP5 during a 1000 s power reduction from 100% to 50% full power yields root-mean-square deviations of 1.71 °C for core outlet temperature and 0.82 kg/s for steam flow rate, demonstrating consistent transient predictions. Open-loop simulations investigate the coupled neutronic and thermal–hydraulic responses to reactivity insertion, feedwater flow and temperature increases, and steam flow reduction. Closed-loop simulations demonstrate stable load-following operation over 60%–100% full power while maintaining primary-loop natural circulation. The developed model provides a flexible foundation for control strategy development and system-level modeling of nuclear cogeneration and integrated energy applications.

title: Coherent structures and flow periodicities in a mixed-geometry tube array
abstract: U-bend and once-through nuclear steam generators (SG) have tube bundles with highly symmetrical array patterns, typically of square or triangular geometry. The interaction between transverse flows and these spatially periodic tube arrays leads to the formation of coherent flow structures in the form of highly organized vortex shedding in the tube arrays. A consequence of this is potentially damaging vortex-induced vibrations (VIV) resonance. For once-through and U-bend steam generators, VIV is characterized by well-defined Strouhal numbers, which are used to calculate potential VIV resonance frequencies for SG design flow-induced vibration analysis. In helical coil heat exchangers, commonly proposed for compact SMRs designs, the planer tube pattern symmetry is broken. Unlike straight tube bundles, the tube arrangement in each cross-section of a helical coil steam generator is not constant but varies along the helix axis. This mixed-geometry pattern consists of combinations of in-line and parallel triangular tube patterns or even more complex geometries. The present work focuses on the effect of symmetry breaking, in two specific azimuthal planes, by studying the flow in the simplified mixed geometry straight tube arrays, constituted of square and triangular tube configurations. We investigate the flow dynamics effect of interactions between coherent flow structures (modes) from the two constituent sub-arrays. The nonlinear mode interaction leads to bifurcations and creation of new coherent structures or flow modes which are generally more complex in spatial form and spectral content. For the square-triangular hybrid array, the resultant dominant coherent flow mode appears as a modified triangular sub-array mode 1 with additional frequency content associated with mode interaction. The square sub-array mode 1 is significantly suppressed and appears to undergo bifurcation in the mixed geometry array. More generally, the flow behavior in the specific mixed-geometry array studied here suggests that VIV analysis for helical tube bundles is significantly more complex. Unlike the pure symmetric array modes, the mixed-symmetry coherent flow modes show strong non-stationarity with time-variable frequency content. The expected implication for VIV is weaker excitation due to the reduced efficiency of energy transfer to the vibrating tubes.

title: Conceptual design of an integral scaled facility for the E-SMR concept based on the Power-to-Volume methodology
abstract: Given the growing interest in integral facilities for SMRs to better understand their associated phenomenology and to validate thermal–hydraulic system codes, this work proposes a scaled integral facility for the theoretical E-SMR model from the ELSMOR project. The scaling is based on the Power-to-Volume methodology and constrained by the use of commercially available stainless steel pipes. The exclusion of ad-hoc piping imposes limitations on preserving the scaled volumes, while the chosen methodology does not allow perfect conservation of the prototype’s hydraulic diameters. After analyzing different alternatives, a non-integral facility with separated tubes was selected to better preserve both hydraulic diameters and volumes. Finally, a RELAP5 model of the conceptual scaled facility was developed and compared with the prototype. Simulations of SBO and SB-LOCA events showed that distortions in the scaled coolant volumes, caused by the use of commercial pipes, and in the volumes of structural components lead to deviations in the transient response. A second IET facility was subsequently proposed to address these limitations, resulting in notable improvements in the representativeness of the facility. Nevertheless, considerable distortions in the scaling of the structural components remained, and their impact on the facility response was found to be non-negligible.

title: Experimental Study of Thermal Radiation in a Large PANDA Vessel with Steam Content Variation
abstract: In this paper, we present an experimental investigation of thermal radiation effects in the PANDA facility (Paul Scherrer Institute, Switzerland), focusing on gas atmospheres with different steam content. Thermal radiation may influence the containment atmosphere temperature and buoyancy, thereby affecting hydrogen distribution during a postulated accident. Two new experiments at initial steam contents of 5% and 30% extend the previously published HYMERES-2 measurements, filling the remaining steam-content gap. The combined dataset comprises five experiments from the OECD/NEA PANDA-1 and HYMERES-2 projects, spanning 0.1% to 60% steam. Particular attention is given to quantifying the post-compression thermal relaxation across this extended range.The containment atmosphere initially consisted of an air and steam mixture at elevated temperature, except for the nearly dry reference experiment, which started at room temperature. A helium-rich layer was established in the upper region to limit convective mixing induced by the subsequent helium injection. Its nominal initial helium concentration was 50%, except in the 30% steam experiment, where it was approximately 100%. The gas mixture was compressed by injecting helium at 10 g/s from the top over 1 200 s. The subsequent gas thermal behavior and concentration distribution were recorded during the compression phase and a 1 800-s decay phase.Higher initial steam contents were associated with lower peak excess temperatures and faster thermal relaxation. Using a common temperature-based criterion for the return toward the initial thermal state, the experiments with 2%, 5%, and 60% steam reached this condition 950, 860, and 540 s after injection stopped, respectively. The nearly dry reference did not reach it during the observation period. The 30% steam experiment reached the criterion after 400 s. These findings have profound implications for computational fluid dynamics calculations in the presence of steam.

title: Nuclear Energy Perceptions among Predominantly Urban and Highly Educated Respondents in Malaysia: Policy Implications in the Context of the 13th Malaysia Plan
abstract: Malaysia’s rising energy demand and net-zero target by 2050 have renewed interest in nuclear power as a low-carbon option under the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan (RMK-13). This study assessed nuclear energy knowledge, perceptions, and support among 400 Malaysian adults recruited through an online non-probability convenience survey. The sample was predominantly urban and highly educated; the findings should not be interpreted as nationally representative. Data were analyzed descriptively and inferentially using Microsoft Excel. The 15-items knowledge assessment indicate that respondents showed reasonable understanding of the basic functions, applications, and operational safety of nuclear energy with 94.3% recognized nuclear power as an alternative electricity source and 79.5% knew that Malaysia has research reactors rather than commercial nuclear power plants. However, 45.8% were unsure or confused about the relationship between nuclear plants and nuclear bombs. Reported dimension means were highest for policy and governance (3.97), followed by the environment (3.76), economy (3.57), and safety (3.55). The overall support mean was 3.83, and 83.8% supported exploring nuclear energy under RMK-13. Support differed significantly by gender (p < 0.001) and education level (p = 0.002). Favorable support scores coexisted with concerns about safety, transparency, and siting in the open-ended responses.

title: Machine-learning-accelerated multi-objective optimization of forward-directed neutron sources via Geant4 simulations
abstract: Designing compact, forward-directed neutron sources requires navigating a vast parameter space. Yield, directionality, and energy often compete, making this a multi-objective challenge that has resisted systematic optimization. We present a machine-learning-accelerated framework that addresses this problem by combining large-scale Geant4 Monte Carlo simulations with a feed-forward neural network emulator and SHAP interpretability analysis. We construct a dataset of 2880 simulated reaction configurations spanning stable beam and target isotopes from hydrogen to aluminum, with 100 million primary ions per configuration. The trained emulator rapidly predicts two figures of merit: the forward neutron flux within a zero-to-fifteen-degree cone about the beam axis, and the corresponding mean neutron energy. Multi-objective optimization over the emulator identifies a Pareto-optimal front that delineates the best attainable trade-offs between these competing objectives. SHAP analysis reveals that beam ions and their energies are the dominant performance drivers. Deuterium beams paired with low-Z targets—such as 6 Li, 7 Li, and 9 Be—consistently populate the Pareto front. Target density, by contrast, exerts comparatively little independent influence. Notably, the emulator achieves its highest accuracy in the region of objective space most relevant to the application: errors are concentrated among configurations with low flux and low energy, which are less desirable by design. Because Geant4 is known to underestimate thick-target neutron yields for certain channels, the reported Pareto-optimal fluxes represent conservative lower bounds. The workflow establishes a general, extensible template for simulation-to-ML neutron source optimization. It also provides a quantitative roadmap for guiding targeted experimental validation.

title: Does information framing matter for nuclear waste acceptance? An experimental test of social comparison, urgency, and intergenerational equity frames
abstract: Public acceptance is a precondition for siting a high-level radioactive waste (HLRW) repository, yet experimental evidence on how disposal information should be communicated is scarce, particularly in East Asia. This study tests whether three theoretically distinct information frames — a precedent from an advanced country, the projected saturation of domestic on-site storage facilities, and the intergenerational burden of unmanaged waste — produce different levels of acceptance of HLRW repository construction in South Korea. A between-subjects experiment with pre- and post-treatment measurement was embedded in a national web survey of Korean adults with quotas matched on region, gender, and age (N = 1,898). Acceptance, perceived risk, perceived benefit, knowledge, and negative affective imagery were measured, and pre–post differences and between-frame contrasts were analyzed using confidence intervals, equivalence tests, and multiple regression. Because the pre- and post-treatment items used different response formats (5-point and 7-point), raw change scores confound genuine attitude change with the mechanical expansion of the response range. On a common 0–100 metric, the average shift was small and slightly negative (−0.84 points, 95% CI [−1.66, −0.02]), while the proportion of supportive respondents increased by 1.0 to 4.0 percentage points. The randomized between-frame comparison, which is unaffected by the change in response format, yields differences of at most 0.06 scale points, with 90% confidence intervals contained well within an equivalence bound of d = 0.20. Perceived benefit is the strongest condition-general predictor of acceptance and of the raw pre–post difference scores, followed by knowledge, whereas perceived risk and negative affective imagery are weak or null. Condition-specific change-score regressions suggest different correlational patterns across the three frames, although the response-format mismatch limits their interpretation as persuasion pathways. The particular frame adopted by a credible message appears to matter far less than the message’s substantive content, but the design does not support strong claims about the magnitude of information-induced attitude change.

title: Cost-informed selection of the lower bound of the gray region in MARSSIM final status survey planning
abstract: Background In MARSSIM Final Status Survey (FSS) planning, the Lower Bound of the Gray Region (LBGR) is often treated as a fixed statistical input, although it also affects remediation burden and survey cost. Methods This study formulates LBGR as a cost-statistical decision variable. For each candidate LBGR, the method calculates relative shift, required FSS sample size, remediation steps, remediation cost, and FSS cost, and selects the feasible candidate with the minimum total cost. A three-regime analysis further evaluates how the initial contamination level relative to DCGL W changes the decision between mandatory remediation, additional remediation, and sampling-only planning. Results In the hypothetical baseline case, the optimized LBGR was approximately 150.0 Bq/g, requiring 15 samples and two remediation steps, with a total cost of approximately 142,500 USD. Sensitivity analyses showed that beta relaxation reduces sample size at the cost of greater Type II error tolerance, whereas sigma reduction changes both sample size and the selected cleanup target. The sample-size calculation was checked against a published MARSSIM example. Conclusion The framework provides a transparent basis for balancing cost, statistical conservatism, data quality, and regulatory defensibility in FSS planning.

title: Reassessing double-ended guillotine break requirements: evidence-based analysis of regulatory assumptions after five decades of nuclear operation
abstract: Nuclear power plant regulations mandate comprehensive protection against the postulated double-ended guillotine break (DEGB) scenarios, involving the instantaneous, complete circumferential severance of the largest reactor-coolant system piping. The DEGB is the largest possible pipe break and it is encompassed by a large break loss of coolant (LBLOCA) accident postulated as a design basis accident for large water reactor nuclear power plants by the U.S. nuclear regulatory guidance. Despite more than 20,000 reactor-years of cumulative global operating experience spanning 35 countries and over 650 reactors that have operated historically, including units that have subsequently been permanently shut down, zero DEGB events have been documented in any domestic or international reporting system. This paper examines the technical, probabilistic, and materials-science evidence underlying the DEGB postulate and evaluates whether it continues to be an appropriate design-basis assumption. Probabilistic fracture-mechanics analyses—including studies commissioned directly by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)—consistently place direct crack-induced DEGB frequencies on the order of 10 −12 per reactor-year, and seismically induced pathways yield frequencies of 10 −7 to 10 −6 per reactor-year, well below thresholds conventionally used to define credible design-basis events. Ductile nuclear piping materials exhibit stable crack-growth behavior that is mechanistically incompatible with instantaneous circumferential severance. International regulatory experience—particularly Germany's four decade implementation of break preclusion and the NRC's approval of leak-before-break methodology for nearly all U.S. pressurized-water reactors—validates that alternatives to DEGB protection maintain safety while significantly reducing economic burden. Current DEGB-driven protection systems impose estimated costs of hundreds of millions of dollars per plant, with fleetwide and global aggregate impacts reaching tens of billions of dollars. This paper demonstrates that the evidence base accumulated over five decades is sufficient to justify removing DEGB from design-basis requirements through formal rulemaking, rather than continuing the current case-by-case exemption approach, and also provides a framework for risk-informed implementation consistent with modern regulatory standards.

title: Simulation Study on the Migration Behavior Characteristics of Radioactive Aerosols with Charge in an Electric Field
abstract: The migration characteristics of charged radioactive aerosols under the action of an electric field were studied. This paper focuses on the situation in which radioactive aerosols carry charges due to the charging effect, which makes up for the shortcomings of related quantitative comparative studies. Based on the theoretical calculation method, the discrete phase model and magneto-hydro dynamics in Fluent software were combined to carry out a numerical simulation of the radioactive aerosol transport process. The effects of three parameters—electric field intensity, radioactive aerosol charge density, and radioactive aerosol particle size—on radioactive aerosol transport were studied. The results show that with the increase of electric field intensity and the charge density of radioactive aerosols, the particle trajectory distribution of radioactive aerosols has a trend of gathering from the bottom to the top of the calculation domain. When the size of radioactive aerosols was 100 μm, the charge density was 0.8(A·s)/m3 and the electric field intensity was 31 000 V/m. The electric field force on radioactive aerosols was approximately balanced with gravity, and the particle trajectory was horizontally distributed. Under the near-force-balance condition of E = 31 000 V/m and a volumetric charge density of 0.8C/m3, particles with diameters of 1, 50, and 100 μm exhibited similar overall vertical positions of the trajectory envelope. This result is associated with the constant-volumetric-charge-density assumption and is limited to the near-force-balance condition examined in this study. The results demonstrate, within the assumptions of the present numerical model, that the charging effect can substantially influence the migration of radioactive aerosols in an external electric field. Independent experimental validation is still required before the model can be used for quantitative engineering prediction.

title: High-Fidelity CFD Simulation of a Turbulent Mixed Convection Axial Flow in a Heated Rod Bundle
abstract: A wall-resolved large-eddy simulation (WR-LES) is carried out with the code_saturne solver to investigate an asymmetrically heated upward flow within a tube bundle configuration. The low-Reynolds number, buoyancy-affected flow is representative of the turbulent mixed convection regime occurring during main steam line break transients. The predictions are assessed against a reference high-accuracy quasi-direct numerical simulation (DNS) database, considered as a numerical experiment. The flow exhibits a range of complex phenomena characteristic of mixed convection, including the growth of a thermal plume associated with strong cross-flows, buoyancy-induced partial laminarization, subsequent turbulence redevelopment, and the formation of a shear-driven mixing layer. Despite the non-trivial nature of the configuration, the LES results show excellent agreement with the quasi-DNS reference, both calculations performed in the frame of the Boussinesq approximation. These results demonstrate the ability of the industrial CFD solver code_saturne to perform high-fidelity simulations to accurately capture buoyancy-affected turbulent structures and transitional behaviors in rod-bundle geometries. The present work provides a solid foundation for future sensitivity analyses and supports the development of upscaling strategies aimed at improving and validating Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes models and subchannel-scale thermal-hydraulic tools used in safety analyses of nuclear systems.

title: High dose-rate response and individual correction of commercial electronic personal dosimeters for nuclear emergency radiation protection
abstract: Reliable active dosimetry is essential during nuclear and radiological emergencies, yet the response of deployed electronic personal dosimeters (EPDs) is rarely verified for every unit in the 1– 7 S v h − 1 regime. Type testing establishes model-level compliance, whereas emergency use depends on individual instruments. We characterised ten commercial silicon-diode EPD units of the same IEC 61526-certified model in a traceable 137 Cs reference field. The units showed high repeatability ( 𝐶 ⁢ 𝑉 < 2 % ) but unit-dependent dose-rate bias, from −9.3% to ＋7.7% at 7 S v h − 1 ; one unit over-responded progressively, which a single dead-time correction cannot reproduce. A device-specific second-order polynomial correction reduced the mean RMSE from 0.187 to 0 . 0 1 1 S v h − 1 and held the residual instrumental non-linearity within ± 1 . 5 % . Applying the first-session coefficients to an independent second session, and predicting intermediate dose rates not used in fitting, both kept residuals within ± 1 . 5 % , confirming temporal reproducibility and out-of-sample validity. Bare-device directional measurements showed up to ≈ 1 9 % lateral response reduction, supporting an optional conservative planning margin ( 𝑆 ⁢ 𝐹 ≈ 1 . 2 ). All corrections were established for a single 137 Cs spectrum and must not be extrapolated to other photon energies without re-calibration. Individual pre-deployment characterisation is a practical complement to model-level type testing for EPDs in nuclear emergency radiation protection.

title: An improved stack-effect model for predicting natural convection characteristics in passive autocatalytic recombiners
abstract: Passive autocatalytic recombiners (PARs) are critical components for hydrogen mitigation in nuclear power plants (NPPs). PARs operate passively, triggering catalytic recombination once hydrogen concentration reaches a specific threshold. Since PAR operation relies on natural convection without an external power, ensuring adequate convective flow is essential for stable performance. This study numerically investigates the characteristics of natural convection within a PAR across various configurations, including catalytic plates temperature, chimney length and the number of plates. The results indicate that increasing these parameters enhances buoyancy forces, leading to a stronger natural convection within the PAR. Based on the numerical simulation results, a novel predictive model is proposed for inflow velocity by refining the conventional stack effect equation. By incorporating geometry-dependent pressure losses into the conventional equation, the proposed model enables a more accurate estimation of natural convection based on design parameters. This modified correlation demonstrates an improved agreement with simulation results, reducing prediction error from 15.86% to 2.51%. As the geometry dependence is carried by the loss terms, a single correction coefficient applies to different PAR configurations without refitting.
